anchorPassages.text:
I pray thee do not wonder if the sight
Of children, given o’er for lost, has made
My converse somewhat long and tedious.
Full well I know the joy I have of them
Is due to thee, to thee and no man else;
Thou wast their sole deliverer, none else.
The gods deal with thee after my desire,
With thee and with this land! for fear of heaven
I found above all peoples most with you,
And righteousness and lips that cannot lie.
I speak in gratitude of what I know,
For all I have I owe to thee alone.
Give me thy hand, O Prince, that I may touch it,
And if thou wilt permit me, kiss thy cheek.
What say I? Can I wish that thou should’st touch
One fallen like me to utter wretchedness,
Corrupt and tainted with a thousand ills?
Oh no, I would not let thee if thou would’st.
They only who have known calamity
Can share it. Let me greet thee where thou art,
And still befriend me as thou hast till now.

anchorPassages.text:
But he hath found asylum. O beware,
And fail not in due reverence to the god.
O heed me, father, though I am young in years.
Let the prince have his will and pay withal
What in his eyes is service to the god;
For our sake also let our brother come.
If what he urges tend not to thy good
He cannot surely wrest perforce thy will.
To hear him then, what harm? By open words
A scheme of villainy is soon bewrayed.
Thou art his father, therefore canst not pay
In kind a son’s most impious outrages.
O listen to him; other men like thee
Have thankless children and are choleric,
But yielding to persuasion’s gentle spell
They let their savage mood be exorcised.
Look thou to the past, forget the present, think
On all the woe thy sire and mother brought thee;
Thence wilt thou draw this lesson without fail,
Of evil passion evil is the end.
Thou hast, alas, to prick thy memory,
Stern monitors, these ever-sightless orbs.
O yield to us; just suitors should not need
To be importunate, nor he that takes
A favour lack the grace to make return.

I read “They only who have known calamity / Can share it” slowly and put it in my own words: He says that only people who have known calamity can share it with someone else. Next, craft. I notice how short the sentence is, and that “known” comes before “share”: experience is the price of sympathy. What do lines 1195–1196 reveal about who can share suffering? Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus asks to kiss Theseus’s cheek, then stops himself: “Can I wish that thou should’st touch / One fallen like me to utter wretchedness” (lines 1191–1192). Gratitude and shame show in the same gesture. A plain statement that Oedipus is grateful would miss how deeply he still sees himself as polluted, even in his best moment.

items.text: How does the conflict in “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)” shape what we understand about the daughters return; a suppliant son?
items.lookFor: The conflict between a father’s loathing and the sacred duty to a suppliant (and the daughter’s plea), and how it frames the coming meeting as a test of whether Oedipus can hear his son.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The conflict is between Oedipus’s loathing, “That voice, O king, grates on a father’s ears” (line 1236), and the god’s claim, since the son “hath found asylum” (line 1238). Oedipus himself just received sanctuary as a suppliant; now his son asks for the same. The conflict makes the coming meeting a test of whether Oedipus will honour for his son the custom that protected him.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “Where, where?”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from the reunion (lines 1153–1172) with their connotations, such as “nurslings,” “Props,” “darlings” or “wayfaring,” showing a father’s dependence and tenderness.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The words “nurslings” (line 1165) and “Props” (line 1167) carry the scene. “Nurslings” makes the daughters little children he has cared for, while “Props” makes them the supports he leans on. Antigone answers “So sorrow sorrow props” (line 1168). The words show that care in this family runs both ways and grew out of shared suffering.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The turn is Theseus’s news of a suppliant at Poseidon’s altar, which turns joy into dread; its likely effect is a hard meeting between father and son that Oedipus agrees to only because his daughter pleads.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The turn is Theseus’s report that “a man, no countryman of thine, / But of thy kin, hath taken sanctuary” (lines 1213–1214). The joy of the reunion drains at once, and Oedipus begs, “Dear friend, forbear, I pray” (line 1226). Because Antigone pleads, he agrees to hear the man, so the next scene will bring father and son face to face, with Oedipus’s hostility already clear.

items.text: How does “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)” build on “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A cause-and-effect link: the ode imagined Theseus winning the daughters back, and this episode confirms it, so Oedipus now owes Theseus everything, which is why he cannot easily refuse Theseus’s request.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode ended with “an escort with the maids draws near” (line 1152). Episode 3 confirms what the elders imagined: Theseus has “brought thee back the maids / Alive and nothing harmed” (lines 1203–1204). Oedipus’s debt, “For all I have I owe to thee alone” (line 1188), makes it hard to refuse when Theseus asks him to respect the suppliant at the altar.

items.text: In “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about the daughters return; a suppliant son, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: A motive behind a claim: Oedipus says he does not know who the suppliant is, then guesses at once and calls him “hateful,” which shows old anger that has been waiting.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus first claims, “Of what thou askest I myself know naught” (line 1212), and wonders, “I marvel who is this petitioner” (line 1223). But at the word “Argos” he knows at once: “My son, O king, my hateful son” (line 1232). The speed of the guess and the word “hateful” show anger that has been waiting; his neutral questions were never really neutral.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (Can you forgive someone and still hold them responsible?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer to the bell-ringer (forgive and still hold responsible) that uses Antigone’s argument: hearing someone is not excusing them, since a bad plan shows itself in open words.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: I first said forgiveness means letting go of blame. Antigone separates the two. She asks her father only to listen: “If what he urges tend not to thy good / He cannot surely wrest perforce thy will” (lines 1244–1245), and “By open words / A scheme of villainy is soon bewrayed” (lines 1246–1247). You can hear someone and still hold them responsible; listening is not excusing.

items.text: Where does theme appear in “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)”, and how does it connect the daughters return; a suppliant son to the larger concern with guilt and intent?
items.lookFor: Where guilt and intent appear: Oedipus calls himself “Corrupt and tainted” though he has argued he acted unknowingly, and he holds his son guilty for deliberate neglect.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus still calls himself “Corrupt and tainted with a thousand ills” (line 1193), so he has not shaken off the stain even after arguing that he acted without knowing. Antigone, though, treats the son’s wrongs as chosen and still calls them “a son’s most impious outrages” (line 1249). The scene sets unknowing guilt, which Oedipus carries, against deliberate wrongdoing, which he will not forgive.

items.text: Is Antigone right that a father cannot repay a son in kind? Defend your view.
items.lookFor: An evaluation of Antigone’s claim (lines 1248–1249) as a principle, with a position and a counterpoint (justice may require consequences; the son’s wrongs were deliberate).
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: mostly right. She argues, “Thou art his father, therefore canst not pay / In kind a son’s most impious outrages” (lines 1248–1249): a parent who answers cruelty with cruelty repeats it, and she points to where “evil passion” ends (line 1257). Counter-line: she does not deny the son’s guilt, calling his deeds “impious outrages” herself, and Oedipus could reply that some harm must have consequences even within a family.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): Antigone is the voice of mercy, as she will be the voice of conscience in Antigone. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand with two lines from Episode 3, with a qualification that her mercy is practical and conditional (hear him; you need not grant his suit), not unconditional forgiveness.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: agree, with a qualification. She is the voice of mercy: “O listen to him; other men like thee / Have thankless children” (lines 1250–1251), and she asks him to let “their savage mood be exorcised” (line 1253). But her mercy is practical. She asks only for a hearing and admits her father need not grant what his son wants (lines 1244–1245). Mercy here means openness, not unconditional pardon.

items.text: Which character in “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)” acts most wisely in the matter of the daughters return; a suppliant son, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard applied to two characters, for example judging by what is owed to a suppliant: Theseus and Antigone honour it, while Oedipus at first refuses. Give a line for each.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of respect for the sacred rights of a suppliant, Theseus acts most wisely. He warns, “O beware, / And fail not in due reverence to the god” (lines 1238–1239). By the same standard, Oedipus at first acts least wisely: “I have come to loathe it. Force me not to yield” (line 1237). A student could rank Antigone highest instead, since she persuades without commanding.

items.text: You are directing “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of the daughters return; a suppliant son.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as the daughters pressing close on either side of their father, or Oedipus stopping his hand short of Theseus’s face, each with its effect.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) On “Cling to me, press me close on either side” (line 1171), let the daughters kneel on either side of the seated Oedipus, so he is literally held up by his “Props” and the picture matches the words. (2) On “Oh no, I would not let thee if thou would’st” (line 1194), have Oedipus reach toward Theseus’s face, then pull his hand back before touching it. The audience sees gratitude stopped by shame.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions answerable from lines 1153–1269: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: Where has the suppliant taken refuge? (At Poseidon’s altar, lines 1214–1216.) Why/how: Why does Theseus not describe the fight himself? (He would rather be known by deeds than words, line 1201.) Should/what if: Should Oedipus have refused to hear his son? (Answers weigh his anger, lines 1236–1237, against the suppliant’s rights and Antigone’s plea, lines 1238–1253.)

items.text: Connect “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)”, with its focus on the daughters return; a suppliant son, to curse and mercy: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about curse and mercy, the question’s theme. The link is strong in prospect: Antigone pleads for mercy toward a son Oedipus loathes, but his response is not yet heard. A strong answer says what must come next.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is strong but still unresolved. The scene sets the daughter’s plea for mercy, “yielding to persuasion’s gentle spell” (line 1252), against her father’s loathing of the son whose voice “grates on a father’s ears” (line 1236). Oedipus yields only grudgingly (lines 1263–1264). To strengthen the link, Sophocles must show whether the hearing Antigone won leads to mercy or to something harder.

items.text: Is the characterization in “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)” effective in presenting the daughters return; a suppliant son, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment against a stated criterion (does the characterization show mixed feelings, or one note?), with a line that meets it and one that might miss it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because Oedipus is shown with mixed feelings in quick succession. He is overjoyed (“Death were not wholly bitter with you near,” line 1170), humbled before Theseus (lines 1191–1194), then bitter toward his son (line 1232). Counter-line: Theseus’s modesty, “I would be famous more by deeds than words” (line 1201), is admirable but very tidy, and a reviewer might find him too perfect to be fully human.

items.text: Compare how “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)” treats the daughters return; a suppliant son with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (a story of a family reunion followed by an unwelcome relative’s return, or the prodigal son) and one thing Episode 3 sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The parable of the prodigal son shows a father running to welcome a son who has wronged him. Episode 3 sees what that story leaves out: a father may not want to welcome the son at all, and a sibling may have to argue him into even hearing it. Here it is the daughter, not the father, who pleads, “For our sake also let our brother come” (line 1243). The play treats mercy as something that may need persuading, not instinct.

items.text: Predict what “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction from two clues, Oedipus’s loathing of his son and his request that no one be allowed to dispose of him, about the mood the elders will sing next, checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: Oedipus agrees to hear his son only grudgingly and calls him “my hateful son” (line 1232). Clue 2: he asks that none “have power to dispose of me” (line 1266), as if he expects pressure. Before the meeting, the elders will probably reflect on the troubles of a long life and an old man’s burdens, so the ode may be dark rather than hopeful. After reading, students check whether the ode matched that mood.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the daughters return; a suppliant son?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core: a newly reunited family learns that an estranged son wants to speak with his father, and a daughter persuades the father to listen. It names two details that must stay.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: A father has just been reunited with the daughters who care for him when a nurse says his estranged son is waiting in the hospital chapel, asking to see him. The father refuses until one daughter persuades him. Two things must stay: the son asking from a protected place (“he hath found asylum,” line 1238), and the daughter’s argument that hearing him costs nothing, since “By open words / A scheme of villainy is soon bewrayed” (lines 1246–1247).

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.
